node.title: Re: Two octal values for eacute?
node.author: haukex
node.doctext:
Please see [https://www.joelonsoftware.com/2003/10/08/the-absolute-minimum-every-software-developer-absolutely-positively-must-know-about-unicode-and-character-sets-no-excuses/|The Absolute Minimum Every Software Developer Absolutely, Positively Must Know About Unicode and Character Sets (No Excuses!)].

The character U+00E9 LATIN SMALL LETTER E WITH ACUTE (é) is encoded in [wp://Latin-1], [wp://Latin-9], and [wp://CP-1252] as the single byte \xE9 (\351), but when encoded with [wp://UTF-8], it's the two-byte sequence \xC3\xA9 (\303\251).

In other words, some of your files are encoded with one of the single-byte encodings, others are encoded with UTF-8, and you'll have to specify the correct encoding when opening them, as in e.g. open my $fh, '<:raw:encoding(UTF-8)', $filename or die "$filename $!"; (see [id://11102684]). That way, when you read the data into Perl, the characters are correctly decoded and you'll always have the correct characters (e.g. "\N{U+00E9}") in your Perl strings.

If you don't know the encoding of the input files, you could use a module like [doc://Encode::Guess], or I've written a tool that tries to be a little smarter: [https://bitbucket.org/haukex/htools/src/master/enctool|enctool] - it allows you to narrow down the guesses by specifying what characters are expected to appear in the input file using e.g. the --one-of='\xE9' option. Some files, like HTML and XML, will often include a definition of the character set in their source, and (except for the cases where that declaration is incorrect) the appropriate parser modules (e.g. [mod://XML::LibXML]) should honor that encoding.

As an aside, if you're putting Unicode characters in your Perl source, you should save it as UTF-8 and add use utf8; at the top of the file. If you're writing Unicode characters to the console, add use open qw/:std :utf8/;. And of course always [id://111088], and a recent version of Perl is strongly recommended when working with Unicode.

If you have further issues with encodings when reading files, please see the tips for posting questions in [id://1233709|this node].

By the way, why are you looking for "é" characters in the first place? Maybe there's a more efficient way to do what you're doing with your regex, if you tell us what the task is.
